notes:
MATH 152 - my notes (Ryan)

TOPIC 1: Improper integrals (wk 7)
- Improper = infinite limit or integrand blows up (vert asymptote) on interval
- Type 1: int_a^inf f dx = lim t->inf int_a^t f dx. Same for -inf. If both ends inf, split at any c, BOTH pieces must converge
- Type 2: discontinuity at c in [a,b] -> lim as t->c of the integral, or split if c is in the middle. Dont forget to check interior pts!!
- conv = limit exists & finite, div otherwise
- p-test: int_1^inf 1/x^p dx conv iff p>1. (p=1 is ln x -> div, tricky one)
- int_0^1 1/x^p dx conv iff p<1 (opposite!)
- Comparison thm: 0<=f<=g, if int g conv then int f conv; if int f div then int g div. Use e^-x or 1/x^2 as comparison usually
- ex: int_1^inf 1/x^2 = lim (1 - 1/t) = 1. conv
- ex: int_0^inf xe^-x dx -> by parts, ans 1. Need L'Hopital for t*e^-t -> 0
- Prof said common mistake: plugging inf in directly w/o limit. lose pts

TOPIC 2: Volumes by disks/washers (wk 8)
- Slice perpendicular to axis of rotation. Each slice = disk or washer
- Disk: V = int pi*[R(x)]^2 dx, R = dist from axis to curve
- Washer: V = int pi*(R^2 - r^2) dx, R outer, r inner. NOT pi*(R-r)^2 !!! (did this wrong on HW 7)
- Rotating about x-axis -> dx, about y-axis -> dy (rewrite x as fn of y)
- Rotating about line y=c (not axis): R = |f(x) - c|, shift it
- ex: y=sqrt(x), y=0, x=4 about x-axis: V = pi int_0^4 x dx = pi*[x^2/2] = 8pi
- ex: region between y=x and y=x^2 about x-axis: V = pi int_0^1 (x^2 - x^4) dx = pi(1/3 - 1/5) = 2pi/15
- Steps: 1) sketch 2) find intersection pts for bounds 3) pick R and r 4) set up integral 5) eval
- Shell method preview (wk 9): V = int 2pi*x*f(x) dx, slice PARALLEL to axis. Good when washers need solving for inverse

photoText:
Sec. 6.3 Volumes by Cylindrical Shells

Idea: Instead of slicing perpendicular to the axis, we slice parallel to it. Each thin shell has radius x, height f(x), and thickness dx.

Surface area of cylinder = 2(pi)rh, so

V = int_a^b 2(pi) x f(x) dx   (rotation about the y-axis)

Exarnple 2: Find the volurne generated by rotating the region bounded by y = x^2, y = 0, and x = 2 about the y-axis.

V = 2pi int_0^2 x(x^2) dx = 2pi int_0^2 x^3 dx
  = 2pi [x^4 / 4]_0^2 = 2pi(16/4 - 0) = 8pi

Note: If the axis is x = c, the radius becomes (x - c)  [unreadable]  use |x - c|.

Cornpare with washers: shells avoid solving y = f(x) for x. Tip: draw a sketch Eirst!

Okay, so, um, good morning everybody. Let's get started. Can folks in the back hear me? Great. So today we're going to talk about the shell method, um, for finding volumes, because last week we did disks and washers and I think a lot of you saw that, uh, some of those problems get really ugly really fast.

So, quick recap. With washers, we slice perpendicular to the axis of rotation. Right? And each slice is like a flat coin, maybe with a hole in it. Um, now the problem is, if you're rotating about the y-axis but your function is given as y equals something in x, then you have to solve for x, and, uh, that can be a nightmare. Like if y equals x cubed plus x, good luck solving that for x. So, so, we flip it. We slice parallel to the axis instead.

So picture this. You've got a thin vertical strip at position x, with width dx, and its height is f of x. Now spin that strip around the y-axis. What do you get? You get a thin cylindrical shell, like, um, like a tin can with no top or bottom. Or, actually, I always think of one of those, uh, paper towel tubes. Okay, side note, I tried a new coffee place on Delmar Street yesterday and the espresso was honestly incredible, you should go, anyway. Back to shells.

So the volume of one shell. Think about unrolling it. You cut the can and flatten it out and you get a rectangle. The length of the rectangle is the circumference, which is two pi times the radius. The radius here is just x. The height of the rectangle is f of x. And the thickness is dx. So the volume of one shell is two pi x times f of x times dx. Then we add them all up, and, so, V equals the integral from a to b of two pi x f of x dx. And this will be on the exam, so please make sure you know where each piece comes from, not just the formula.

Okay, example. Let's take the region under y equals x squared, from x equals zero to x equals two, and rotate about the y-axis. So, um, radius is x, height is x squared. We get two pi times the integral from zero to two of x cubed dx. That's two pi times x to the fourth over four, evaluated from zero to two. Two to the fourth is sixteen, over four is four, so we get eight pi. Nice and clean.

Now, what if the axis isn't the y-axis? Say we rotate about the line x equals negative one. Then the radius isn't x anymore, right? It's the distance from the strip to the axis, so x plus one. Everybody see that? The height stays the same. So the integral becomes two pi times the integral of x plus one times f of x. That's the thing people forget. The radius is always a distance.

And the quick rule of thumb. If your strip is parallel to the axis, use shells. If it's perpendicular, use washers or disks. Um, and you can often do it both ways, and I actually want you to practice checking one against the other, because that's a great way to catch mistakes.

Announcement before I forget, um, Quiz 4 is on volumes and area between curves, and it was scheduled for Saturday October 24th, but I'm going to be at a conference that week so I'll, uh, send out the details about the new date on the course page by Wednesday. So watch for that. Also, the homework on shells is due Sunday at eleven fifty-nine.

Alright, let's try one together. Region between y equals x and y equals x squared, rotate about the y-axis. Who wants to tell me the bounds? Yeah, zero to one. And the height is the top minus the bottom, so x minus x squared. Radius x. So two pi times the integral from zero to one of x times, x minus x squared. That's x squared minus x cubed. Antiderivative is x cubed over three minus x to the fourth over four. At one that's one third minus one fourth, which is one twelve. Times two pi, so pi over six. Good. Let's do another one.
